title: 3 Critical Classroom Management Strategies For The First Hour Of The First Day Of School -of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin condenses the first hour of a new school year into three sequential moves. 'Give' means opening with warmth — smile, openness, genuine happiness at meeting each student — which invokes the Law of Reciprocity and builds early likability. 'Show' means demonstrating the classroom management plan with emphatic tone and body language rather than simply reading it aloud, signaling that it matters. 'Teach' means delivering one focused, high-energy academic lesson on a single objective rather than easing in with something 'light and fluffy,' since real teaching in the first hour sets the tone for rigor all year. He describes the three as legs of a stool: together they establish trust, set non-negotiable boundaries, and shock students out of months of unstructured time into purposeful engagement.
points: Open the first hour with visible warmth and genuine enthusiasm to trigger the Law of Reciprocity.
Present the classroom management plan with demonstrative tone and body language, not a flat read-aloud.
Teach one real, focused academic lesson on a single objective during the first hour — not a 'light and fluffy' activity.
These three moves function together as a foundation: they establish trust, set boundaries, and shock students into purpose.
How you use the first hour of day one shapes how easy classroom management will be to maintain the rest of the year.
quotes: The quicker you set a culture of kindness, respect, and high-bar work expectations, the easier it will be to maintain.
From the moment you first greet your students, give of yourself—your smile, your openness, and your genuine happiness that each of them is a member of your class.
No, you must show its importance through your emphatic tone and body language and enthusiasm for its purpose.
You must teach the heck out of it. The lesson must be clear and detailed and focused on a single objective, on one thing you want your students to be able to do or to know.
These three, like legs on a stool, provide the foundation upon which you can create the best learning experience your students have ever experienced.
They shake the rust off months of being cooped up or stuck on the couch without purpose. They give them meaning and responsibility and something to look forward to.
